title: The first question (Berakhot 2a)
hookLine: the whole Talmud opens by asking from when the evening Shema may be said
last: NOBODY STARTS AT THE TRUE BEGINNING.

cards: How would you open a book people would study for centuries? With God, maybe. With creation, or the meaning of life.
The Talmud, the giant library of Jewish law and argument, opens with a question that sounds almost like a text to a friend. From what time can you say the evening Shema? That's the first line.
No grand speech, no introduction. Just a practical question about tonight. And it turns out to hold a whole way of seeing time.

teach.b: The Shema is the line at the heart of Jewish prayer, Hear, O Israel, said morning and evening. The Torah says to speak these words "when thou liest down, and when thou risest up."
So the rabbis asked: lying down begins when, exactly? The Mishnah answers: from the time the priests go in to eat their holy food, at nightfall. And until when?
Three answers. Rabbi Eliezer: until the end of the first watch of the night. The sages: until midnight.
Rabban Gamliel: until the first light of dawn. Then a story.
Rabban Gamliel's sons came home late from a wedding feast, past midnight. We haven't said the Shema yet, they told him. He said: if dawn hasn't come, you still can, and you still should.
Then the Talmud asks a question about the question. Why start with evening, and not morning? One answer: the verse itself says lying down first, then rising up.
Another: in the story of creation, evening comes first.
"And there was evening and there was morning, one day." That's the order the tradition follows. A Jewish day, Shabbat and every holiday begins in the evening, not at midnight or sunrise.
The day starts in the dark and grows toward light. So the Talmud's first question isn't small at all. It asks you to notice the exact moment one day becomes the next, and to meet it with words.

how: Observant Jews say the Shema in the evening prayer (Maariv) after nightfall and again at bedtime, and every Jewish day, including Shabbat and the holidays, begins at sundown.

games.q: who said what about the evening Shema — tap the pairs.
p: until the end of the first watch
until the first light of dawn

s: the Talmud opens with a question about the evening Shema
its first line asks from what time the evening Shema may be said.
a Jewish day begins at midnight
it begins at sundown: there was evening and there was morning.
Rabban Gamliel told his sons it was too late after midnight
he told them: until dawn comes, you still can.

games.q: you're Rabban Gamliel. your sons come home from a wedding after midnight: we haven't said the Shema yet. what do you tell them?
o: if dawn hasn't come, say it now.
skip tonight and say it twice tomorrow.
games.why: he tells them that until the first light of dawn they still can, and still should. the night isn't over until morning comes.

practice: Think back over the last few days: when does your evening really begin, when you close the laptop, when the kids are asleep, when the light outside changes color, when your phone finally goes face down?
Picture meeting that moment on purpose, with one breath or one line you care about. If you pray, it could be the Shema; if not, it could simply be noticing: the day is turning.

wordCard.voice: Shema, the line at the heart of Jewish prayer. The Talmud's first question asks from when the evening Shema may be said, and answers: from nightfall, because in the Torah the evening comes first.
